name: Hash Chain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Linking Records So the Past Cannot Quietly Change
lesson.summary: A hash chain embeds each record's hash inside the next record, so altering anything in the past breaks every hash that comes after it.
lesson.body:
A cryptographic hash function takes data of any size and produces a short, fixed length fingerprint. Two properties matter most here. First, the output changes unpredictably even for a tiny change in input, an effect often called the avalanche effect. Second, it is computationally infeasible to find two different inputs that produce the same output, or to work backward from an output to recover the input. Data integrity checking already uses single hashes this way: store a file's hash, recompute it later, and a mismatch tells you the file changed. A hash chain extends that idea across a whole sequence of records instead of just one.

The construction is simple but powerful. Each record in the chain includes, as part of its own input, the hash of the record immediately before it. So the hash of record three is not just a function of record three's content, it is a function of record three's content combined with the hash of record two, which itself depended on the hash of record one. Written out, h3 = H(data3, h2) and h2 = H(data2, h1). This nested dependency is what gives the chain its name and its strength.

Consider three simple log entries: "Alice paid Bob 10," "Bob paid Carol 4," and "Carol paid Dave 2." Each entry is hashed together with the previous entry's hash to produce the next link. If someone later tries to change the first entry to "Alice paid Bob 100," the hash of that entry changes. But the second entry's hash was computed using the original hash of entry one, so the second entry's stored hash no longer matches what you get by recomputing it. The third entry's hash is wrong too, and so on down the line. One quiet edit in the past becomes a visible break in every link after it.

This is why hash chains matter for data integrity beyond a single file check. A log, a document history, or a sequence of transactions can be verified as a whole by walking the chain and recomputing each hash, confirming it matches the one stored in the next record. You do not need to trust whoever assembled the chain, you only need the hash function's properties to hold and you need a trustworthy copy of the final hash, often called the chain's tip, to compare against.

It is worth being precise about what a hash chain actually proves. It proves that the records, once entered, have not been altered relative to each other. It does not prove the first entry was true when it was written, and it does not prevent someone from tampering with data before it is hashed. A hash chain is a detector of after the fact changes, not a guarantee of original honesty. That distinction becomes central in the next chapter, where we ask more precisely what it means for a structure to be tamper evident rather than tamper proof, and later when Merkle trees show how to organize many records more efficiently than a single straight line.
